Mme. Sarah Grand.
Mmo. Sarah Grand, otherwise Mrs. M'Fall, has been staying at Folkstone for a change after illness, but has now returned to her residence at Bath (observes the "Star.") She writes steadily, mostly in the morning, as she thinks this is the best time, and she takes a keen interest in social work. The author of "The Heavenly Twins" and other novels, which attained fame about a quarter of a century ago, is also fond of travelling, and she knows the East well. But apart from these interests, Sarah Grand has no special hobbies, except a great love for all things Irish, Ireland being the land of her birth though her father was an English naval officer. As a young girl in her middle teens she became the wife of Colonel M'Fall, an Army doctor over twice her age, who left her a widow many years ago.

A "manless" passenger train, run and controlled entirely by wireless, is announced by Mr. G. Y. Allen, of the American Westinghouse Electric and Manufacturing Co., says a message to the Paris edition of the "New York Herald." It is now entirely feasible, by a combination of automatic and radio supervisory control from a central office, said Mr. Allen, to start a train without a crew, run it at full speed over clear tracks, slow it down or stop it in accordance with the signals of an automatic block-signalling system, start it up again, and open its doors. The wireless features of this system, according to Mr. Allen, are of the "carrier current" type—radio waves which travel along the power lines of the railway instead of spreading out through the ether, as in ordinary broadcasting. The waves, using this system, can be directed to any desired point, and can be utilised to operate switches and other devices, as well as to carry on conversations.—"Daily Express."

The thyroid gland in the neck, consisting of two lobes and an isthmus, joining them across the windpipe, creates a unique substance, mostly consisting of iodine. Without it none can live. Without enough of it in the blood of an expectant mother, not only is she imperilled, but her baby cannot be born normal. The thyroid gland, if starved of iodine, tries to make bricks without straw, enlarges and nearly dies in consequence. We call that result goitre; astonishing evidence has come from University College, London, suggesting that there is a relation between goitre and cancer. The right course for us is to restore the missing iodine to our own food, so that our thyroids can live and work for us as they should. In my view, the State
and the municipalities, notably through education authorities and maternity centres, should see that we are all supplied with iodine at almost costless rates. This will undoubtedly save a vast amount of uglines, idiocy, deaf mutism, and, possibly, cancer.—Dr. G. W. Saleeby, in the "Daily Herald," Air Navigation.

The subject of practical navigation of aircraft was dealt with in a paper prepared by Captain F. Tymms and read at a meeting of the Royal Aeronautical Society. He was impelled by his own experience, he said, and that of others to the conclusion that the air must follow the sea and the aeroplane the ship rather than the iron-bound train, that these questions were of vital importance in the future of aviation. In discussing the question of maps, it was pointed out that there was a fairly general view that a map for aerial navigation should be a picture of the earth as seen from an aeroplane. That was an eminently sound principle, but if carried too far that particular principle would result in a map which would be very difficult to read because of the crowded nature of the information and the diverse appearance of similar things. One was forced to the conclusion, said Captain Tymms, that a map for aerial navigation must follow in general the principles on which all maps were produced—that surface features must be shown by conventional signs.—"Daily Telegraph." A New Substitute for Glass.

The latest chemical discovery is a substitute for glass, made from purely organic materials. It seems to have many attractive properties, being much softer than glass, so that it can be worked on a latho into all sorts of required shapes. It can be coloured for decorative purposes, but the most interesting thing about it is that its "refractive index" can be varied over a wide range, making it very suitable for optical instruments and capable of replacing very expensive kinds of glass in telescopes and microscopes. Another interesting optical point is that it appears to be much more transparent than glass to the invisible rays—ultra-violet and infrared light. It may be a surprise to those who have not heard of synthetic resins to hear that this glassy substance is made by condensing formaldehyde and urea. At first a kind of soft, transparent jelly is obtained which with the aid of a little heat and addition of traces of some sodium salts is converted to a hard glassy material which has the properties already described. It will probably cheapen optical appliances to an unheard-of degree and supersede the expensive fluorite lenses of apochromatic objectives and may find therapeutic application as a substitute for glazing in hospitals.

Although cafeterian are used by everyone in America, rich and poor, alike, it is to the business girl that they are of special benefit (says a "Daily Telegraph" writer.) The time she spends over her meals is entirely within her own control, so that she has often more than half her free hour to herself, and, in addition to this, the fact that very little service is needed in a cafeteria reduces the cost of food considerably. In nearly every one the process is the same, and the visiting Englishwoman soon slips into the habit, so simple it is, and so practical. When you enter the room you are faced with a long counter-piled with plates of food, and presided over by about half a dozen attendants, whose duty it is to replenish the dishes as required. Generally there is a railing about four feet away from the counter, so that you cannot stray out into the room until you have been given an account of your just debts, and immediately in front of the counter is another railing along which you slide your tray. You pick this up at the door where you find it all ready waiting for you, complete with a table napkin folded round two forks a spoon, and a knife. Once you have secured this, you embark on the rapturous process of sliding your tray along and choosing your lunch from the goodly selection before you. At the very end of the counter you will come to the coffee and tea urns, and here, too, if you are in a very-up-to-date cafeteria, you will find yourself faced with a selection of hot dishes. As you leave the counter you submit your well-laden tray to the inspection of the girl at the cash desk, who adds up the cost of your dishes, and gives you a check for the amount, which you pay at the door on leaving. You are then free to choose a table and settle yourself down to your meal. It is all done very quickly. At the most it is five minutes from the time you enter the door until you are seated at your table, and you may leave the minute you finish. There is none of that process so well known in England of "catching the waitress's eye." By the cafeteria system, too, labour is reduced to a minimum, for, in addition to the attendants behind the food counter there are only about four waiters in the room itself, who gather up your tray and used dishes when you have finished, and refill the water jugs on every table. Even this is often unnecessary, for the newest cafeterias are generally supplied with a fountain of iced water in the middle of the room, and beside it will be more often than not, a glass holder for cardboard cups, which you fill yourself, thus achieving a nice sense of independence, which adds materially to the flavour of your meal.
